why.correct: 29/50 = 58% at 2 minutes and 41/50 = 82% at 10 minutes on the moist half; the control halves stayed between 23 and 27 of 50, close to 25.
options: At 2 minutes the moist half held 29 of 50 (58%), barely more than half, and the count kept rising to 41.
Correct: a steady rise on the moist half, with no drift in the control dishes.
Control half 1 went 26, 23, 25, 27, 24: it wandered around 25 with no trend.
The moist-half count rose at every count, from 29 to 41; it never fell back toward 25.

why.correct: χ² ≈ 20.5 is far above 3.84, so a split as uneven as 41 to 9 would be very unlikely by chance alone. The test supports a response to moisture but says nothing about how the animals sense it.
options: A chi-square value above the critical value means the null hypothesis is rejected, not kept.
The test shows the distribution is not random; it gives no information about which sense organs are involved.
Correct: 20.5 > 3.84, so the deviation from 25:25 is statistically significant.
A null hypothesis is never accepted, and the control dishes are a different comparison; the moist-dry counts differ strongly from 25:25.

why.correct: With the same paper on both halves, any gathering on one side would come from something other than moisture, such as a slope, a draft or the light. The controls stayed near 25:25, so moisture is the likely cause in the test dishes.
options: The control dishes contain no moist half, so they add no moist-dry comparisons.
Every dish held 10 animals anyway; equal numbers are not what the control dishes add.
Dead animals would still be counted on one half, and dishes without a moist half cannot compare survival on moist and dry paper.
Correct: the controls rule out a side preference unrelated to moisture.

why.correct: This is a kinesis: dry conditions raise activity and speed, moist conditions lower them. Animals wander until they happen onto moist paper and then stay. The border test shows no steering toward moisture.
options: Correct: a change in activity, not aimed movement, explains the gathering.
Steering (a taxis) is ruled out: animals released on the border walked into the dry half first as often as into the moist half.
Nothing in the data tests learning, and a simple change in activity already explains the counts.
The halves add up to 50 animals at every count, so animals on the dry half were counted; they moved over to the moist half.

why.correct: Species A flowers with long nights, so it is a short-day plant. With 10 hours of dark only 3% flower; with 12 hours, 80% do. The critical length lies between those two.
options: With 12 hours of dark, 80% of species A already flowers, so the critical night is shorter than 12 hours.
Species A flowers when nights are long and days are short, the pattern of a short-day plant.
Correct: the jump from 3% to 80% happens between 10 and 12 hours of dark.
Species A flowers well with 12 and 14 hours of dark too (80% and 95%), not just with 16.

why.correct: Rows 5 and 6 differ in only one way: a 5-minute flash splits the 16-hour night into two 8-hour nights. The day is still 8 hours, yet flowering falls from 98% to 0%. So the plant is measuring the unbroken night.
options: Rows 1 and 5 change the day and the night together, so they cannot separate the two.
Correct: same day length, different unbroken night, very different result.
Both rows have long nights and both flower; they do not separate day from night.
These rows show that far-red reverses red, which is about the light detector, not about day versus night.

why.correct: Phytochrome is switched on by red light and off by far-red. A red flash makes the plant read the night as broken (A stops flowering, B flowers); far-red right after cancels it (A flowers, B does not). The last flash wins.
options: Correct: a reversible pigment switch explains why the last flash decides the result.
Ten minutes of light hardly changes the day; rows 6 and 7 get the same total light but opposite results.
In row 7, species B does not flower (5%), so far-red light does not make every plant flower.
Species B flowers after the red flash, so red light does not damage flowering; the pattern fits a switch, not damage.

why.correct: Short-day plants respond to the longest unbroken dark period. A dark break during the day leaves the 16-hour night intact, so species A should flower as in row 5.
options: Correct: the night, not the day, is measured, and the night is still unbroken.
Interrupting the day with darkness does not stop flowering; interrupting the night with light does.
The plant does not add dark periods together; it responds to the longest one, here 16 hours.
Row 3 had a 12-hour night, which is why 80% flowered; here the night is 16 hours long.

why.correct: Temperature is a possible confounding variable: many plants flower differently when warm or cold. Holding it constant means the differences between rows come from the light treatments.
options: Correct: it removes temperature as an alternative explanation.
Holding temperature constant does not make results equal; the light treatments still gave 0% to 98%.
Phytochrome is switched by red and far-red light, not by a particular temperature.
With temperature constant there is no daily warming to sense; the plants measured darkness.

why.correct: Short-day plants measure the unbroken night with phytochrome. Red light in the night switches phytochrome on, so the plant reads two short nights and does not flower; the day itself is unchanged.

variables.name: Percentage of plants that form flowers
variables.why: The flash splits the 15-hour night into two 7.5-hour periods, shorter than the critical night length, so flowering is blocked.

variables.name: Amount of active phytochrome in the leaves just after each flash
variables.why: Red light converts phytochrome to its active form, which had been slowly reverting during the dark.

variables.name: Length of the light period at the start of each day
variables.why: The flash comes in the night; the daytime light period is still 9 hours.

variables.name: Longest stretch of unbroken darkness the plants receive
variables.why: It falls from 15 hours to about 7.5 hours, because the flash cuts the night in half.

why.correct: Each cycle lasts 24 hours plus 18 minutes. 18 ÷ 60 = 0.3 hour, so the period is 24.3 hours. In constant conditions the internal clock runs at its own pace; daily light would normally reset it to 24 hours.
Innate behavior appears complete without experience: the isolated spider never saw a web, and the stickleback's attack is a fixed action pattern triggered by the red cue.
options: Innate: the spider had no chance to learn the web from others.
Learned: operant conditioning, an action linked to its reward.
Learned: classical conditioning, a neutral sound linked to food.
Innate: a fixed action pattern set off by a simple cue, even on a crude model.
Learned: the crow's response depends on one past experience with one person.

why.correct: On the comb, straight up stands for the direction of the sun, so the angle of the run from vertical is the angle of the food from the sun. A longer waggle run means a greater distance.
options: The dance is referenced to the sun, not to a compass direction.
Longer waggle runs code for greater distances, so this food is farther than 500 m.
Correct: angle from vertical gives the angle from the sun; run length gives distance.
A run to the left of vertical means food to the left of the sun's direction, not the right.

why.correct: Foraging ants lay a trail pheromone, a chemical signal, and nestmates follow it. Wiping erased the chemical over the strip only, so the trail resumes beyond it.
options: Ants on either side of the strip are still visible, yet the ants lose the trail only on the wiped part.
Correct: a pheromone trail explains why only the wiped strip confuses them.
The ants wander and then cross the strip; they do not turn back to the nest.
Ants lose the trail only where the chemical was wiped, which a sun compass does not explain.

why.correct: This is kin selection. The call is risky (altruistic), but relatives carry copies of the same alleles. Calling more when kin are near is what inclusive fitness predicts.
options: Selection does not favor alleles because they help the species; and the data show calling depends on kin nearby, not on the colony.
Calling puts the caller at risk, and nothing in the data shows age or learning; the difference tracks relatives nearby.
The percentages are per predator approach, so they already account for how many predators each female saw.
Correct: the behavior tracks the presence of relatives, as kin selection predicts.

why.correct: The squirrel first turns down its metabolism, and as its body cools, reaction rates fall further, so it needs little ATP. Low oxygen use shows that cellular respiration, and so the use of stored fat, has slowed but not stopped.
options: Oxygen use is 3% of normal, not zero, so respiration continues slowly; 4 °C slows enzymes rather than denaturing them.
The drop in oxygen use reflects lower demand, not a better supply of oxygen.
Fat stores more energy per gram than glucose, and hibernators live mainly on fat.
Correct: a lower metabolic rate stretches the fat store over the whole winter.

why.correct: Only blocking light at the tip stopped bending, and covering the lower shoot did not, so the tip senses light. The bend happens lower down, so a signal (auxin) must travel from the tip.
options: Covering the lower shoot did not stop bending, so light on the lower shoot is not needed.
The capped shoots grew straight up, so growth continued; only the bending stopped.
Correct: sensing at the tip, response below it.
Shoots with clear caps bent toward the light, so a cap as such does not stop the response.

why.correct: Food and temperature never changed, yet the birds showed migratory restlessness in the right seasons and directions. Day length, the one seasonal cue they received, was enough. (Many birds also have an internal yearly clock that day length keeps in step; this design cannot separate the two.)
options: The birds were kept indoors, and the timing followed the light schedule they were given.
Food was constant all year, so food shortage cannot explain the timing.
The restlessness came in the migration seasons and faced the migration direction, so it matches migration.
Correct: the only seasonal cue was day length.

why.correct: The tip detects the light, auxin is moved to the shaded side and carried down, more auxin makes those cells elongate more, and the unequal growth bends the shoot toward the light.
Imprinting is learning during a brief sensitive period soon after hatching; the attachment formed then lasts and even affects later mate choice.
options: Habituation is a fading response; here a strong, lasting attachment formed.
Correct: a lasting attachment learned in a short early window.
Nothing in the description involves a reward, and imprinting needs none.
No red cue is involved, and the goslings' attachment depended on what they saw first.

why.correct: Flashes are visual signals, and because each species has its own pattern and females answer only theirs, the patterns keep matings within a species.
options: Light flashes are visual, not chemical, and females answer only one pattern.
Each species has one pattern, and females respond to it; nothing suggests family-by-family learning.
Correct: species-specific courtship signals.
Females answer the flashes of their own species, so the flashes do play a part in mating.

why.correct: 13,800 ÷ 24,000 × 100 = 57.5%. The phytoplankton capture 24,000 kJ (gross primary productivity) and keep 10,200 (net primary productivity).
82 ÷ 1,020 × 100 = 8.04%, which rounds to 8.0%. Using the energy taken in (410 ÷ 4,100) would give 10%, but trophic efficiency compares what is stored at each level.
Energy stored in phytoplankton biomass that zooplankton do not take in either is never eaten or is eaten but not absorbed. Both end up as detritus, the food of decomposers.
options: Phytoplankton respiration is already subtracted: 13,800 kJ was released as heat, leaving 10,200 stored.
Energy is not destroyed; digestion breaks molecules down so they can be absorbed.
Correct: uneaten algae and undigested food feed the decomposers.
Energy taken in already includes everything the zooplankton absorb, fat stores included.

why.correct: Endotherms spend most absorbed energy on respiration that produces body heat (39.2 of 40 kJ here), leaving little for growth. Ectotherms like the fish do not pay that cost.
options: Correct: the cost of endothermy shows up as heat released by respiration.
Energy is never destroyed, and trophic level alone does not explain why one animal stores 20% and another 2%.
The comparison already uses energy taken in (absorbed), so differences in digestion are not part of it.
Fat is stored biomass and would be counted in the last column, not as heat.

why.correct: If it stored a share like the small fish (about 20%), it would store about 8 kJ, ten times as much. An ectotherm's body temperature follows the water, so less of its food is burned for heat.
options: Trophic level sets how much energy is available (40 kJ), not what share an animal stores.
Correct: ectotherms store a larger share of what they take in.
The data show fish storing 20% of their intake; nothing suggests a fish's swimming costs exceed an endotherm's heat production.
The birds at this level already store 0.8 kJ, so a fourth level can store energy.

why.correct: Each year CO₂ peaks in May (423.8, then 426.2 ppm) and bottoms out in September-October (418.6, then 421.0 ppm), and every month is higher in year 2 than in year 1.
options: CO₂ falls from May to October within each year, and January of year 2 (422.4) is higher than January of year 1 (420.0).
The peak is in May and the low in September-October; and year 2 is higher than year 1.
Correct: a yearly cycle on top of a rising trend.
The concentration changes every month, falling for five months in a row, not in one sharp drop.

why.correct: Most land, and so most land plants, is in the Northern Hemisphere. In the growing season, photosynthesis removes more CO₂ than all respiration returns; in winter the balance reverses.
options: The ground is not a sink that fills with summer CO₂; the seasonal change follows plant growth.
Correct: net uptake by northern plants during the growing season.
Decomposers release CO₂ by respiration; they do not remove it.
Hibernation happens in winter, and animal respiration is small next to plant uptake.

why.correct: May of year 2 (month 17) is 426.2 ppm and May of year 1 (month 5) is 423.8 ppm. (426.2 − 423.8) ÷ 1 year = 2.4 ppm per year. Comparing the same month removes the seasonal cycle.
Burning carbon stored for millions of years, and cutting forests that held carbon, add CO₂ faster than photosynthesis and the oceans take it up, so the yearly mean climbs.
options: Correct: people move carbon from long-term reservoirs into the air.
Nothing in the data describes the station's temperature, and a monitoring site far from cities measures air mixed over a large area.
Overall the oceans take up CO₂ from the air rather than adding it.
The station is chosen to be far from local sources, and volcanoes add far less CO₂ each year than human activity.

why.correct: Less land means fewer plants, so the seasonal uptake and release are smaller, and the southern growing season is in the other half of the year. Air mixes between hemispheres within about a year, so the long-term rise is shared.
options: The yearly swing comes from land plants, not from the ocean, and southern seasons are reversed.
The seasons are reversed and the plant cover is smaller, so the swing differs in size and timing.
CO₂ added anywhere spreads around the globe, so the rising trend appears there too.
Correct: smaller swing, shifted by half a year, same trend.

why.correct: The bacteria are chemosynthetic producers. The worms supply them with hydrogen sulfide, oxygen and CO₂ and live on the organic molecules they make.
options: Little organic matter reaches 2,500 m, and the worms have no gut to take in food.
Correct: chemosynthesis makes these bacteria the producers.
Heat cannot be turned into chemical energy by organisms; the energy comes from a chemical reaction.
Decomposers recycle matter but cannot be the energy source for a whole community.

why.correct: Respiration uses 0.60 × 3,500 = 2,100 g. NPP = GPP − respiration = 3,500 − 2,100 = 1,400 g of carbon per m² per year.
Respiration (by decomposers, here) and combustion both oxidize carbon compounds and release CO₂.
options: Photosynthesis takes CO₂ out of the air.
Releases CO₂: decomposers respire the carbon in the leaves.
Burial stores carbon away from the air; slow decay is why peat and coal form.
Releases CO₂ from carbon stored in the coal for millions of years.
Shell building takes carbon out of the water and locks it in solid carbonate.

why.correct: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the nodules convert N₂ into ammonium the soybean uses; when soybean roots and stubble decompose, ammonium (and nitrate made from it) is added to the soil for the corn.
options: Plants cannot use N₂ themselves; fixation is done by bacteria in the nodules.
The benefit of beans in a rotation comes mainly from added nitrogen, not from saved phosphorus.
Correct: symbiotic nitrogen fixation enriches the soil.
Denitrification removes usable nitrogen, which would hurt the corn, and plants do not denitrify.

why.correct: Blocking one step of a cycle makes the substance before it pile up and the substance after it run down, while other cycles are unaffected.

variables.name: Ammonium in the soil
variables.why: Ammonium from decomposers and fixation keeps arriving, but it is no longer converted to nitrate.

variables.name: Nitrate in the soil
variables.why: No new nitrate is made, while roots and bacteria keep using the nitrate already there.

variables.name: Nitrate washed from the soil into a nearby stream
variables.why: Less nitrate in the soil means less is carried away in water; ammonium binds to soil particles more than nitrate does.

variables.name: Phosphate in the soil
variables.why: Phosphate comes from weathering and decomposition, not from nitrification, so blocking nitrification does not change it.

why.correct: Eating mayfly larvae (primary consumers) makes a sunfish a secondary consumer; eating dragonfly larvae (secondary consumers) makes it a tertiary consumer.
options: Snails eat only algae, so they are primary consumers; being eaten does not change their level.
Crayfish eat only snails, so they feed at one level (secondary consumers).
Dragonfly larvae eat only mayfly larvae, so they feed at one level.
Correct: two kinds of prey at two different levels.

why.correct: Biomass is a snapshot; energy flow is a rate. Small, fast-dividing producers can support a larger standing mass of consumers because they replace themselves many times a year.
options: Correct: high turnover keeps the energy pyramid upright even when the biomass pyramid is inverted.
Zooplankton are animals that eat phytoplankton; they do not photosynthesize.
No level can get more energy than the level below stored; the rule holds in water too.
No level can pass up more energy than it received; efficiency cannot exceed 100%.

why.correct: Unlike carbon and nitrogen, phosphorus has no important atmospheric reservoir; phosphate is released slowly from rock and recycled by decomposers.
options: There is no phosphorus gas for bacteria to fix; that describes nitrogen.
Correct: rock and sediments are the main reservoir.
The atmosphere holds very little phosphorus.
Burning fossil fuels mainly releases carbon dioxide, not phosphorus.

why.correct: Trees pull water from deep soil and release it as vapor through their leaves. Without them, much of the rain runs off instead of returning to the air, so less moisture is carried downwind.
options: Correct: transpiration supplies much of the vapor for rain over land.
Bare soil usually lets more water run off, and water in the soil does not add to the clouds.
Bare ground generally reflects more sunlight than a dark forest, and evaporation from the farms is not what changed.
Water in the cut wood is a small, one-time amount and does not explain a lasting drop in rain.

why.correct: Neither animal changed mass, so nearly all the food energy was used, mostly in respiration. The endothermic mouse used over ten times as much, because it makes heat to hold its body temperature well above 20 °C.
options: Better digestion cannot explain a ten-fold difference; the lizard simply needs less energy.
Both kept the same mass, so neither added much tissue.
Correct: the cost of endothermy.
The mouse's mass did not change, so it did not store the extra food as fat.

why.correct: Fixation must come first because nothing else can use N₂; nitrification makes nitrate from ammonium; the plant takes it up and builds organic molecules; only then can a consumer get the nitrogen by eating.

Decomposers, like all organisms, release the energy of their food as heat through respiration. Producers can capture light (or chemical) energy, but not heat, so energy must keep entering from the sun.
options: Decomposers respire most of what they absorb; that energy leaves as heat.
Energy is conserved; it changes form to heat rather than being destroyed.
Producers capture light energy and store it; they do not dump an energy surplus.
Correct: heat is a form producers cannot capture.

why.correct: Species R falls from 1,000 (log 3) to 20 (log 1.3) by 10% of its life span: 98% die very young. After that the curve declines slowly.
options: That describes species P, a Type I curve.
That describes species Q, a Type II curve.
Correct: a steep early drop, then a long slow tail.
Species R is the Type III curve, but the number dying is not constant: 980 die by 10% of the life span and only 10 more by 20%.

why.correct: At 50% the value is 1.5, so survivors = 10^1.5 = 31.6, about 32 of the 1,000. A log value of 1.5 lies between 10 (log 1) and 100 (log 2), but not halfway in actual numbers.
On a log scale, equal drops are equal fractions. A drop of 0.3 means survivors are multiplied by 10^−0.3 ≈ 0.5 each interval: about half of those still alive die, whatever their age.
options: Correct: a constant fraction (about 50%) dies in each interval.
Numbers dying shrink as survivors shrink: about 500 in the first interval (1,000 to 501) but only about 1 in the last (2 to 1).
The chance of dying is the same at every age; a straight log line has no late steep drop.
About 500 die in the first 10% and about 1 in the last 10%, far from equal numbers.

why.correct: A Type III curve fits a life history of many small, uncared-for offspring: nearly all die young, and huge numbers are needed for a few to reach adulthood.
options: Correct: Type III survivorship goes with many small offspring and little care.
A songbird with a Type II curve typically lays a few eggs and feeds its chicks.
High survival of the young (Type I) goes with few offspring and much care, not thousands of eggs.
Late, compressed deaths (Type I) go with few, well-cared-for young.

why.correct: Protection removes the main early causes of death, so many more reach 20%; after release they face wild conditions, so the curve then declines slowly, as the wild one does.
options: Hatcheries protect young fish; nothing suggests tanks kill more than the wild does.
Correct: the early steep drop is mostly removed; later mortality is unchanged.
Survival depends on conditions as well as genes; protecting young changes it.
After release the fish die at the wild rate, so survival does not stay high until old age.

why.correct: dN/dt = B − D = 293 − 68 = 225 beetles per week. Check: week 4 starts with 450 + 225 = 675 beetles.
Per capita rate = (B − D) ÷ N = 225 ÷ 450 = 0.50 per week: each week the population adds half its size.
B − D is 100, 150, 225, 338 and 506 in weeks 1 to 5, but (B − D) ÷ N is 0.50 every week. A constant per capita rate times a growing N is exponential growth.
options: The per capita rate is 0.50 in every week; the total rate rises because N rises.
100 are added in week 1 but 506 in week 5.
Correct: constant per capita rate, rising dN/dt.
Food was replaced each week and both rates show no fall: the per capita rate stays at 0.50.

why.correct: During week 5, dN/dt = 0.50 × 1,013 = 506.5 beetles, so N ≈ 1,013 + 506.5 ≈ 1,519 (or 1,520). The table gives the same result: 1,013 + 658 − 152 = 1,519.
Exponential growth requires a constant per capita rate. That holds only while crowding, food or wastes do not raise deaths or lower births; in 10 more weeks there would be over 80,000 beetles.
options: The growth in the table happened at a constant 30 °C; no rising temperature was needed.
Correct: unchanged per capita rates need plentiful resources.
r_max stayed at 0.50 throughout; no change in the beetles was needed for the growth seen.
Births already rose from 130 to 658 because there were more beetles; constant births would slow growth.

why.correct: Total = 40 plants in 10 m², so the mean density is 4.0 per m². 4.0 per m² × 400 m² = 1,600 dandelions.
Competition for water spaces the survivors out: wherever a seedling is too close to an adult, it loses. Uniform dispersion comes from neighbors pushing each other apart.
options: Correct: competition between neighbors produces uniform spacing.
Seeds falling near the parent would give a clumped pattern, but the seedlings there die.
The bushes are evenly spaced, not randomly scattered.
Seedlings close to adults die, so being close together does not help them.

why.correct: Only the mushrooms gather around a patchy resource, the rotting log.
options: Clumped: the food (the log) is in one patch.
Uniform: each bird keeps a fixed distance from its neighbors.
Random: seeds land with no pattern on an even surface.
Uniform: competition for water spaces the shrubs out.

why.correct: Semelparity is a single, all-out reproduction followed by death.
options: Reproducing every year is iteroparity.
Reproducing repeatedly over life is iteroparity.
Several broods over several years is iteroparity.
Correct: one reproductive event, then death.

why.correct: Recovery depends on how fast survivors can reproduce. X's early maturity and huge clutches give a very high r_max; Y adds few young each year and recovers over decades.
options: Better survival of young does not make up for producing one young every 2 years.
Correct: r-selected traits mean fast recovery after a disaster.
Equal losses do not mean equal recovery; their growth rates differ enormously.
Five percent of a population can still reproduce; X especially can rebuild quickly.

why.correct: r-selected species put their energy into fast, plentiful reproduction, which gives a high r_max.
options: r-selected: early breeding raises r_max.
r-selected: many small offspring.
K-selected: long lives go with slow reproduction.
K-selected: heavy investment in few young.
K-selected: late maturity lowers r_max.

why.correct: dN/dt = B − D. Raising D past B makes the growth rate negative, so the population declines, while the birth rate is unchanged.

variables.name: Population growth rate, dN/dt
variables.why: It falls from 600 − 400 = +200 to 600 − 700 = −100 voles per year.

variables.name: Number of voles one year later
variables.why: With dN/dt negative, the population shrinks, to about 1,900 instead of growing to 2,200.

variables.name: Per capita birth rate
variables.why: Births stay at 600 per 2,000 voles, 0.30 per year; the disease changes only deaths.

why.correct: dN/dt = r_max N = 0.03 per minute × 4,000 cells = 120 cells per minute.
dN/dt = r_max N. With the same r_max, dN/dt is proportional to N, so A, 100 times larger, adds 100 times as many per day. Per capita, both grow at r_max.
options: Both are growing exponentially at the same r_max, so resources are not limiting either one yet.
The same r_max means the same per capita rate, not the same number added.
Correct: same per capita rate, numbers added proportional to N.
r_max is a property of the species under ideal conditions; both share it.

why.correct: Change = births − deaths + immigrants − emigrants = 120 − 90 + 0 − 40 = −10, so 500 − 10 = 490 lizards. Using B − D alone (+30) would miss the emigrants.
You need the field's area to plan and scale; quadrats must be placed before plants can be counted; the counts give a mean density; the density times the area estimates the total.
With 999 of 1,000 dying young and the survivors living for decades, the curve drops steeply early and then flattens: Type III.
options: Long-lived adults are part of the story, but Type I also needs high survival of the young.
Survival is very low early and high later, not constant.
Burying the eggs is the only care, and most young still die.
Correct: a steep early drop, then a long tail.

why.correct: Hares peak in years 4 and 13; lynx peak in years 5 and 15. Both cycle with a period of about 9-10 years, and the lynx lag the hares.
options: Correct: same period, lynx lagging hares.
This reverses the order: each lynx peak follows a hare peak.
Lynx range from 2 to 24 per 100 km², a twelve-fold change.
The peaks are offset: hares in year 4, lynx in year 5; hares in year 13, lynx in year 15.

why.correct: In year 4 there are 60 hundred = 6,000 hares and 15 lynx per 100 km². 6,000 ÷ 15 = 400 hares per lynx. Forgetting the hundreds gives 60 ÷ 15 = 4.

Lynx depend on hares for food. When hares are abundant, more lynx survive and breed, but adding new lynx takes a breeding season or two, so lynx numbers peak after hares. Then many lynx and scarce winter food drive hares down, and lynx follow.
options: Correct: the predator responds to its food with a breeding delay.
The graph shows lynx peaks after hare peaks, not before.
Nothing in the data points to weather, and the lynx depend on hares, which explains the lag directly.
Lynx are meat-eaters; they eat hares, not the hares' plants.

why.correct: Removing lynx (fencing) and adding food, alone and together, separates the two causes. If the claim were true, fenced areas would not crash even without extra food.
options: More of the same records shows the pattern again but cannot separate lynx from food as the cause.
Correct: a manipulative experiment that changes one factor at a time.
Body mass could hint at food shortage but does not test the role of lynx directly.
More frequent counts describe the cycle in more detail without changing either cause.

why.correct: Without lynx, hares grow until food becomes the limiting resource. Crowded hares eat their winter food faster than it regrows, so numbers fall back and fluctuate around what the food supply can carry.
options: A population cannot stay above what its food supports; food becomes limiting.
Hares are food for lynx; lynx do not support the hares' plants.
Correct: food, a density-dependent factor, still limits the hares.
Lynx catch many hares, so removing them lets the hare population grow at first.

why.correct: From day 10 the standard cultures stay between 480 and 503 cells per mL, overlapping error bars: growth has stopped, so K ≈ 500 cells per mL.
options: Growth was fast around day 6, which is near K/2, not K.
That is the double-food cultures' level, a different environment with a different K.
Correct: the plateau gives K.
Half the plateau is K/2, where growth is fastest; K is the plateau itself.

why.correct: dN/dt = 0.8 × 250 × (500 − 250)/500 = 0.8 × 250 × 0.5 = 100 cells per mL per day. N = 250 is K/2, where logistic growth is fastest.

The increase was 17 cells per mL from day 0 to 2, 79 from day 2 to 4, 169 from day 4 to 6, 164 from day 6 to 8, then 46 and 23. The fastest change comes as density passes about 250, K/2: a balance of many cells and enough food.
options: The per capita rate is highest early, but with only 5-22 cells per mL few cells are added.
Correct: growth is fastest near K/2.
Near K each cell has little food, so births barely exceed deaths; only 23 cells per mL were added.
From day 14 to 16 the density hardly changed (494 to 498).

why.correct: Food is the limiting resource: twice the food supports about twice as many cells (plateau about 980-1,000 cells per mL). The first days are nearly identical (22 vs 25 on day 2, 101 vs 108 on day 4), so r_max did not change.
options: Early densities are almost the same, so r_max is about the same; the two plateaus differ.
From day 6 the error bars are far apart (for example 434 ± 30 vs 745 ± 40 on day 8).
The double-food cultures level off from day 12 (982, 1,003, 991).
Correct: more of the limiting resource means a higher K.

why.correct: Food amount is the independent variable; everything else that could affect growth, such as starting density, volume and temperature, must be held constant.
options: Food is the variable being tested, so it must differ.
Correct: controlled variables.
The final density is the result (a dependent variable), not something to hold constant.
The day-16 count is a result the experiment measures, not a condition to control.

why.correct: Disease spread and competition for nest holes both act more strongly, on a larger fraction, as the population becomes denser.
options: Density-dependent: crowding speeds transmission.
Density-independent: the frost kills a similar fraction at any density.
Density-dependent: more birds per hole means a larger share go without.
Density-independent: fire burns habitat whatever the density.
Density-independent: flooding kills regardless of crowding.

why.correct: A density-independent loss pushes the herd further below K, where each deer has more food, so the herd grows faster back toward an unchanged K.

variables.name: Number of deer
variables.why: 40% of 800 died, leaving 480.

variables.name: Food available per deer
variables.why: The same plant supply is shared by fewer deer.

variables.name: Population growth rate, dN/dt
variables.why: At 480 deer, (K − N)/K = 0.52 instead of 0.2: with r_max = 0.4, dN/dt rises from 64 to about 100 deer per year.

variables.name: Carrying capacity of the reserve
variables.why: The plants recovered fully, so the reserve can still support about 1,000 deer.

why.correct: dN/dt = 0.4 × 900 × (1,000 − 900)/1,000 = 0.4 × 900 × 0.1 = 36 rabbits per year. Near K the growth rate is small even though N is large.
dN/dt = 0.4 × 1,200 × (1,000 − 1,200)/1,000 = 0.4 × 1,200 × (−0.2) = −96 rabbits per year. Above K the factor (K − N)/K is negative, so the population shrinks.
Intraspecific competition: mass per plant falls steeply with density, while total mass rises only from 48 to 77 g as it approaches the limit set by the pot's resources.
options: Correct: competition for limited resources, a density-dependent effect.
Nothing in the data supports this, and the result is explained by shared resources.
Mean mass per plant fell, which shows the plants grew less, not just that fewer sprouted.
Total mass per pot rose with density (48, 66, 77 g), so crowding did not reduce it.

why.correct: This is overshoot: births responded to past plenty, the herd rose above K, and overgrazing destroyed the slow-growing food, so K itself fell and the population crashed far below its peak.
options: Correct: overshoot plus damage to the food supply.
A population at K stops growing; it does not crash by itself.
Food shortage is density-dependent and can cause a crash, especially when the food itself is destroyed.
A herd that grew from 20 to 3,000 has many young adults; age is not the explanation.

why.correct: K is the population size that the available resources can sustain.
options: Correct: the definition of K.
That is r_max, the intrinsic rate of increase.
Logistic growth is fastest at K/2, not at K.
K is for one population, not the whole community.

why.correct: Shared resources mean less for each individual, raising competition, so the per capita growth rate falls toward zero.
options: A growing population is mostly young; the slowdown comes from crowding, not age.
Organisms do not limit reproduction to save resources; crowding lowers births through hunger and stress.
Resource production need not fall; the same resources are split among more individuals.
Correct: density-dependent changes in births and deaths.

why.correct: The fraction killed by wolves rises with moose density (4%, 9%, 15%), while snow kills a similar fraction (5-6%) at every density.
options: What matters is whether the fraction killed changes with density; for wolves it rises.
Snow killed a steady fraction, about 6%; more individuals died only because there were more moose.
Correct: compare fractions across densities.
Size of the effect does not decide the category; the trend with density does.

why.correct: Density dependence is about the fraction affected. The frost kills about 40% at either density, so it is density-independent.
options: More aphids died in number, but the same fraction; that is density-independent.
Correct: the fraction killed does not change with density.
The frost killed the same fraction at both densities, so competition is not what decided who died.
A frost can kill a large share; it is classified by whether the share depends on density.

why.correct: Plenty of food allows near-exponential growth; more deer mean less food each; hunger lowers births and raises deaths; the per capita growth rate shrinks; growth stops near K.
Owls take a larger fraction of voles at high density, a density-dependent effect that slows vole growth when voles are crowded and eases off when they are scarce.
options: The fraction changes from 2% to 10%, so it depends on density.
Owls kill up to 10% of voles a month, which certainly affects vole numbers.
Removing voles does not increase the food or space the grassland provides.
Correct: a density-dependent factor pulling numbers down when they are high.

why.correct: Woodland Y has 8 species to X's 6, but species 1 makes up 120 of its 160 beetles; X's catch is spread fairly evenly.
options: X has 6 species and Y has 8, so Y is richer.
Correct: higher richness, low evenness.
Richness is the number of species (6 and 8), not the number of individuals.
Y is richer but far less even, and its D (0.43) is lower than X's (0.81).

why.correct: Relative abundance = 120 ÷ 160 × 100 = 75% of the beetles caught in woodland Y.
Diversity combines richness and evenness. In Y, two beetles picked at random are often both species 1, so D is low; X, with fewer species spread more evenly, is more diverse.
options: Richness is only one part of diversity; evenness matters too.
D is a probability that two random beetles differ in species; it does not count rare species.
The question asks about the beetle data, which were collected the same way in both woodlands.
Correct: the index reflects evenness as well as richness.

why.correct: With species 1 at 20 of 60 beetles instead of 120 of 160, no species dominates, so two random beetles are more likely to differ: D rises (to about 0.81).
options: D depends on the shares of each species, not the total number caught.
Richness is unchanged, but evenness rises, and D measures both.
Correct: higher evenness, higher D.
D is a probability, so it cannot exceed 1.

why.correct: Rare species turn up as more individuals are sampled; holding effort constant makes richness and diversity comparable.
options: Correct: equal sampling effort is a controlled variable.
The equal totals (160 each) happened in this study; equal effort does not guarantee them.
Nothing in the setup says beetles are active only in June; effort is controlled to make the samples comparable.
D can be calculated for any sample; the two woodlands here even have different species lists.

why.correct: Alone, A plateaus near 400 and B near 250 cells per mL. Together, A reaches about 375 while B peaks at 80 on day 6 and falls to 4 by day 20.
options: Correct: A persists slightly reduced; B is excluded.
A together reaches 375, close to its 400 alone; B falls to 4, not to half of 250.
Both level off by about day 10 when alone; together it is B that declines.
B grown with A falls to 4 cells per mL, far below 250.

why.correct: This is competitive exclusion: two species with the same limiting resource cannot coexist for long; the more efficient competitor, A, keeps the bacteria too scarce for B.
options: Both species eat bacteria; nothing indicates that A eats B.
Correct: interspecific competition for one limiting resource.
The setup says both eat the same bacteria, with the same ration in every tube.
The setup states they share the same food, which explains the result without any special waste effect.

why.correct: Feeding in different parts of the tube divides the resource (resource partitioning), so competition is weaker and both coexist, though each usually somewhat below its density alone because some overlap remains.
options: Exclusion needs the same limiting resource; the two species use partly different food.
Nothing suggests B is the better competitor here; partitioning lets both persist.
Correct: partitioning allows coexistence.
Some bacteria are shared, so competition is reduced but not zero.

why.correct: The single-species tubes are controls: B reaches 250 cells per mL alone, so its collapse with A cannot be blamed on the medium, the food ration or the temperature.
options: Each group already had five tubes; the alone groups are controls, not extra replicates.
Correct: the alone cultures are the baseline for comparison.
Early growth is similar in both species; the purpose is a control for the whole experiment.
The alone tubes are separate tubes; they do not affect food in the shared tubes.

why.correct: Only the egrets gain while their partner is neither helped nor harmed (+/0).
options: Commensalism: egret +, cattle 0.
Parasitism: tapeworm +, dog −.
Mutualism: bee + (food), flower + (pollination).
Resource partitioning between competitors, not a +/0 symbiosis.
Predation: lion +, zebra −.

why.correct: Removing the top predator sets off a trophic cascade: each level below changes in the opposite direction to the level above it. Inputs from outside the food web are unaffected.

variables.name: Number of minnows
variables.why: Their main predator is gone, so more minnows survive and breed.

variables.name: Number of zooplankton
variables.why: More minnows eat more zooplankton.

variables.name: Amount of phytoplankton
variables.why: Fewer zooplankton graze on the algae, so the algae grow faster than they are eaten.

variables.name: Phosphate carried into the lake by streams each year
variables.why: The streams' phosphate comes from the land around the lake; removing fish does not change it.

why.correct: In Batesian mimicry a harmless mimic gains protection by resembling a harmful model that predators have learned to avoid.
options: Müllerian mimicry needs both species to be harmful; the hoverfly is harmless.
Bright stripes stand out rather than blend in; they work by resemblance to wasps.
Correct: harmless mimic, harmful model.
The hoverfly is harmless; its stripes are a bluff, not an honest signal.

why.correct: This is Müllerian mimicry. Each bird must sample some butterflies to learn the pattern; when two species share it, that cost is split between them.
options: Correct: shared learning cost among harmful species.
A species that stopped being toxic would be a Batesian mimic; the benefit to both comes from shared learning.
Different species generally do not interbreed, and similar patterns do not require it.
Both species taste bad; the shared pattern protects both rather than steering birds to one.

why.correct: This is character displacement: where both species live, natural selection favors individuals that compete less, so beak sizes, and the seeds eaten, move apart. Resource partitioning results.
options: Beak depth is largely inherited; practice does not reshape it.
Correct: selection by competition leads to resource partitioning.
The beaks moved in opposite directions, which fits divergence driven by competition, not a shared change in seeds.
Hybrids would blur the species together, not push their averages apart.

why.correct: A can live lower down (its fundamental niche includes the lower rocks) but does so only when B is absent, so B's competition shrinks A's realized niche.
options: The realized niche can only be the same as or smaller than the fundamental niche.
A survives well on the lower rocks once B is removed.
The experiment tests A on the lower rocks; it says nothing about B on the high rocks.
Correct: removing the competitor reveals more of A's fundamental niche.

why.correct: With richness fixed, diversity rises only if evenness rises.
options: Correct: higher evenness, same richness.
Dominance by one species lowers evenness and diversity.
A new species changes richness, which the question holds constant.
Doubling each species keeps every share the same, so diversity is unchanged.

why.correct: The deer feeds on part of the shrub without killing it (herbivory, +/−); the tick lives on the deer and feeds on it without killing it (parasitism, +/−).
options: Predation kills the prey; neither the shrub nor the deer is killed.
The shrub gains nothing from being eaten, so the first is not a mutualism.
The shrub loses tissue it must regrow, so it is harmed, not unaffected; the tick harms the deer.
Correct: both are +/− but neither kills its partner.

why.correct: A change at the base (more phosphate, so more algae) passed up the food web in the same direction at each level: bottom-up control.
options: The change started at the bottom, with nutrients, not with a predator at the top.
In a cascade levels alternate; here they all rose together.
Correct: nutrient supply limits the levels above.
Algae and fish do not compete for the same resource; fish depend on them through the food web.

why.correct: The cascade runs from the top down: pike reduce minnows, which frees zooplankton, which then reduce phytoplankton, and less algae means clearer water.
Losing the weasels removes one source of deaths, so rabbits should increase in the short term, even if foxes later eat somewhat more rabbits.
options: Correct: release from one predator.
Foxes may eat more rabbits, but they cannot make up at once for all the weasels' kills, let alone catch every rabbit.
Foxes did not change, but weasels did; fewer rabbit deaths means more rabbits.
Weasels eat rabbits; they do not protect them.

why.correct: D is the chance that two random individuals are different species. Near 0, almost every pair is the same species, so one species makes up nearly the whole community.
options: Many evenly common species give D close to 1.
Many rare species, with none dominating, give a high D.
Correct: near 0 means one species dominates.
D describes the community at one time; it does not measure a rate of loss.

why.correct: Control plots held 15-16 species throughout; removal plots dropped each year: 15, 14, 12, 10, 9, 8, 7.
options: The control plots did not decline; they varied between 15 and 16.
Correct: a steady fall only where the sea stars were removed.
The removal plots lost 1 species in year 1 and kept declining to 7.
Removal plots lost species as mussels spread, ending at 7 against 15 in the controls.

why.correct: The sea star keeps mussels, the strongest competitor for space, in check. Mussel cover rose from 20% to 85%, and the species that lost their space disappeared: competitive exclusion released by removing the predator.
options: Correct: the predator held down the dominant competitor.
The data show mussels taking over the rock, not prey starving.
Removing sea stars by hand is a small disturbance; the steady rise in mussel cover explains the losses better.
Nothing in the data points to nutrients, and the loss tracks the spread of mussels.

why.correct: Sea stars were under 1% of the animals counted, yet removing them cut species numbers by more than half: an effect far larger than their abundance, the mark of a keystone species.
options: Foundation species are abundant; the sea star is scarce.
Correct: a small share of the community with a large effect.
The sea star acts by eating mussels, not by building or reshaping the habitat.
The sea star eats mussels; it is their predator, not a competitor for space.

why.correct: A rare species without a key role leaves little gap; its loss lowers richness by about one, while the mussels are still held down by the sea stars.
options: The steep loss came from releasing the dominant competitor; a rare seaweed does not hold mussels back.
A rare species is unlikely to be a strong competitor, so removing it frees little space.
Mussels filter food from the water; a rare seaweed is not their food, and sea stars still eat them.
Correct: losing a non-keystone species has a small effect.

why.correct: From 1 to 16 species, biomass rose (180 to 380 g per m²), drought loss fell (78% to 33%) and recovery after two years rose (62% to 101%).
options: Both trends are reversed: more species meant more biomass and a smaller loss.
Recovery was more complete with more species (101% vs 62%).
Correct: higher productivity, resistance and resilience with more species.
Losses ranged from 78% to 33%, a large difference.

why.correct: They lost 33% of 380 g per m², keeping 67%: 0.67 × 380 = 254.6, about 255 g per m². (The 1-species plots kept 0.22 × 180 ≈ 40 g per m².)
1 species: 68-88%; 16 species: 27-39%. No overlap, so they clearly differ. 8 species: 34-48% overlaps 27-39%, so those two are not clearly different.
options: The intervals 34-48% and 27-39% overlap, so this difference may be due to chance.
The intervals 68-88% and 27-39% are far apart.
Correct: compare the ± 2 SE intervals for overlap.
Error bars that do not overlap, such as those for 1 and 16 species, indicate a clear difference.

why.correct: Species differ in how they cope with drought. The more species a plot has, the more likely some are deep-rooted or drought-tolerant and can take over, so the plot as a whole loses less and recovers faster.
options: Shading may help a little, but the plots still lost a third of their biomass, so the drought did reach them.
Correct: differences among species buffer the whole community.
Diverse plots produced more biomass, not less, so their plants were not growing more slowly.
The design gave every plot the same treatment; nothing suggests extra watering.

why.correct: If the 16-species plots always held a particular hardy species, it could be that species, not diversity, that reduced losses. Random draws spread every species across plots of every diversity level.
options: Correct: randomization separates the number of species from the identity of particular species.
Random choice of species does not set plant numbers; that is controlled by how the seeds are sown.
Choosing the hardiest species on purpose would bias the comparison, the opposite of randomizing.
Placing diverse plots in wet spots would confound the result; the species draw does not do that.

why.correct: Beavers change the physical environment, turning a stream into a pond and wetland that many other species then use.
options: Beavers are few; their effect comes from building, not from being abundant.
Beavers are consumers; the pond's energy comes from its plants and algae.
Beavers eat bark and plants; their effect is not through predation on a competitor.
Correct: a species that creates habitat by changing the physical environment.

why.correct: Keystone species are identified by an effect out of proportion to abundance: X, at 2% of biomass, halved richness.
options: A species that is abundant and has a modest effect fits a dominant species, not a keystone.
Lowering richness does not rule out a keystone role; X's effect is huge for its size.
Correct: small share, large effect.
Nearly any removal changes a community a little; Y's effect is in line with its large share.

why.correct: Elephants act as ecosystem engineers, holding back trees. Without them, the savanna moves toward woodland, and the species that depend on open grassland decline.

variables.name: Number of trees
variables.why: Young trees are no longer pushed over and eaten, so more of them grow up.

variables.name: Area of open grassland
variables.why: Growing trees shade out grass and take over space that was open.

variables.name: Number of grazing zebras and wildebeest
variables.why: Less grass means less food for grazers.

variables.name: Yearly rainfall on the reserve
variables.why: Rainfall is set by regional weather, not by elephants in one reserve.

why.correct: Ecosystem services are benefits that natural ecosystems provide to people, such as pollination and water filtration.
options: An ecosystem service: wild pollinators raise crop yields.
A human industrial process, not a service from an ecosystem.
An ecosystem service: wetlands clean water.
A purchase, not a benefit an ecosystem provides.
Built infrastructure; a floodplain wetland doing the same job would be a service.

why.correct: With no genetic diversity, a pathogen that can infect one plant can infect them all; a varied population would likely include some resistant plants.
options: Growth rate is not the issue; susceptibility was shared by every plant.
Plants do have defenses, and some banana varieties resist this fungus; this one did not.
Infected cuttings can spread the fungus, but clean plants in infected soil fell ill too; no plant could resist it.
Correct: no genetic variation, no resistant individuals.

why.correct: Different kinds of ecosystem in a region are ecosystem diversity, the broadest level of biodiversity.
options: Genetic diversity is variety of alleles within a species.
Evenness describes how equally individuals are spread among species.
Relative abundance is one species' share of the individuals in a community.
Correct: a variety of ecosystems.

why.correct: D combines richness and evenness. Q's higher D shows that two random corals there are far more likely to be different species, so Q is more diverse despite fewer species.
options: Richness is only part of diversity; P is dominated by one species.
Their D values (0.52 and 0.95) differ widely.
Correct: higher D, higher diversity.
Q has the higher diversity index, which, if anything, suggests greater stability.

why.correct: When several species do the same job, the others can take over if one is lost. The fig has no stand-in during the dry season, so its loss affects every animal that depends on it.
options: Position in the food chain does not decide importance; having no stand-in does.
Correct: a unique role makes a species hard to replace.
The other two bird species still eat the same insects, so insects stay in check.
Species differ in how replaceable they are; losses are not equal.

why.correct: Reef-building corals are foundation species: their structure is the habitat many fish shelter, feed and breed in. As dead coral erodes, those fish lose their habitat and decline.
options: Correct: losing a foundation species removes the habitat others need.
Corals and reef fish largely use different food; the corals' main effect is to provide habitat.
The fish depend on the coral habitat, so they are affected even though the heat did not harm them.
Reef-building corals grow slowly; recovery takes many years, not one.

why.correct: Resilience is the speed and completeness of recovery after a disruption; lake A recovered in two years against seven.
options: Correct: faster recovery is resilience.
Evenness describes how equally species are represented, not recovery.
Carrying capacity is for one population; the data are about recovery time.
Trophic efficiency is energy passed between levels; the data do not measure it.

why.correct: Keystone species are defined by an outsized effect relative to abundance, often as predators; foundation species are abundant and build the habitat.
options: Correct: effect relative to abundance versus abundance and habitat.
Keystone species are often predators, and foundation species are often producers such as kelp or trees.
This swaps the two: foundation species are the abundant ones.
Changing the physical environment defines an ecosystem engineer; foundation species matter as habitat, not just as food.

why.correct: Biodiversity covers the variety of alleles within species, of species in communities and of ecosystems in regions.
options: Correct.
These are trophic roles in an ecosystem.
These describe species diversity, one level only.
These are levels of ecological organization, not of biodiversity.

why.correct: Chlorophyll rises from 2.2 to 11 µg/L at 3 km; there afternoon oxygen is 13.5 mg/L and dawn oxygen 3.1 mg/L, the widest gap. Farther downstream all three return toward upstream values.
options: Afternoon oxygen and algae rise below the outfall; only dawn oxygen falls.
Correct: the algae peak matches the largest day-night swing in oxygen.
Dawn oxygen falls (to 3.1 mg/L) while afternoon oxygen rises.
Algae rise five-fold, and dawn oxygen recovers after 3 km.

why.correct: 13.5 − 3.1 = 10.4 mg/L. Upstream the difference is only 9.0 − 8.4 = 0.6 mg/L.
Photosynthesis adds O₂ only in light; respiration by algae, bacteria and animals uses it all the time. Where algae are dense, the daytime gain and the nighttime loss are both large.
options: Photosynthesis releases O₂; the readings are highest in the afternoon, not at dawn.
The swing is largest at 3 km, not at the outfall, and it tracks the algae, not the farm.
Temperature was 19-20 °C at every site, and warm water actually holds less O₂, not more.
Correct: photosynthesis by day, respiration around the clock.

why.correct: Upstream water has not received the farm's nutrients, so it acts as a control: changes below the outfall can be compared with it.
options: Correct: a reference site unaffected by the outfall.
The farm's water enters at distance 0 and flows downstream, so the nutrients do not reach upstream.
The algae drift with the current; the upstream site is not about algae moving.
Upstream oxygen is among the highest dawn readings, not the lowest.

why.correct: If phosphorus limits the algae, removing it shrinks the bloom. Fewer algae, and less dead algae for decomposers, mean less O₂ used overnight, so dawn O₂ rises toward upstream values.
options: Decomposers feed mainly on dead algae; fewer algae means less decay and less O₂ used, not more.
Correct: cutting the limiting nutrient shrinks the bloom and its oxygen demand.
Extra nitrogen does little when phosphorus is the limiting nutrient.
Temperature was the same at every site, yet dawn O₂ varied with algae, so algae matter.

why.correct: 4.5 ÷ 0.9 = 5.0. At each step up this food chain, PCB concentration rises several-fold.

This is biomagnification. Persistent, fat-soluble PCBs stay in the body; since only about 10% of food becomes new tissue, each predator eats far more prey than its own mass and keeps the PCBs from all of it.
options: PCBs are industrial chemicals; animals do not make them.
The water holds only 0.000004 ppm; drinking cannot explain 4.5 ppm in trout, which take in PCBs mainly in food.
Correct: storage plus the large amount of food eaten.
PCBs break down slowly everywhere; faster breakdown would lower concentrations, not raise them.

why.correct: 90 ÷ 0.000004 = 22,500,000, which is 22.5 million times higher. A toxin barely detectable in water can reach harmful levels at the top of a food web.
Biomagnification turns a tiny concentration in water into a high one in top predators; harm happens where the concentration is high, such as in gull eggs.
options: The water level is low, but animals at the top of the food web are exposed to far more.
Correct: the risk is at the top of the food web.
Low levels in producers fit biomagnification; they do not show the top predators are safe.
The water level (0.000004 ppm) is lower than in phytoplankton (0.02 ppm).

why.correct: Long-lived top predators hold PCBs accumulated over years in their fat and keep eating prey that still carry them, so their levels fall slowly. Short-lived plankton are replaced quickly by new, cleaner individuals.
options: Phytoplankton live days to weeks, so new cells soon reflect the cleaner water.
Fast reproduction replaces zooplankton quickly, so their levels drop sooner.
Correct: long life and fat storage keep PCBs in top predators.
The stem says the water levels fall within a few years; PCBs are fat-soluble, not water-soluble.

why.correct: Invasive species often thrive because they leave their natural enemies behind, while native species have not evolved defenses or competitive responses to them.
options: The stem says native mussels declined after the zebra mussels spread, so they were present.
Zebra mussels are small; their success comes from fast reproduction and few enemies, not size.
A trip in ballast water does not change a species' fertility for generations.
Correct: release from natural enemies.

why.correct: Ocean acidification: the oceans absorb CO₂, which lowers pH and reduces the carbonate that corals, oysters and some plankton need.

variables.name: pH of the seawater
variables.why: More CO₂ dissolves and forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺, lowering pH.

variables.name: Carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻) available to shell-building animals
variables.why: Extra H⁺ combines with carbonate to form bicarbonate, leaving less carbonate.

variables.name: Rate at which oysters build their shells
variables.why: With less carbonate, building calcium carbonate shells takes more energy and is slower.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each oyster's cells
variables.why: Seawater chemistry does not change a species' chromosome number.

why.correct: Warming shifted one event (caterpillar hatching) but not the other (egg laying set by day length), so the peak in chick demand misses the peak in food: a timing mismatch caused by climate change.
options: The caterpillar peak is earlier, not longer; the chicks miss it.
The birds lay at the same date, and incubation length is set by the parent's body heat; the chicks do not catch up two weeks.
Correct: a mismatch between food supply and chick demand.
Nestlings need caterpillars; adults switching food does not feed the chicks.

why.correct: Fragmentation makes populations small and isolated, so chance events wipe them out and they are not refilled from nearby; small patches are also mostly edge, unsuitable for deep-forest species.
options: Some farmland birds may enter, but forest birds decline mainly because their patches are too small.
Nothing suggests birds breed faster in small patches; small populations are lost by chance and edge effects.
Small patches get as much sunlight per area; the difference is size, isolation and edge.
Correct: small populations plus edge effects.

why.correct: Cod take several years to reach breeding age, and although each female lays millions of eggs, almost all die young; while they were scarce other species took over their role and some ate young cod, so the population has grown back slowly.
options: Correct: slow maturity plus a changed community.
Fishing removes individuals; the surviving cod can still reproduce.
Ending fishing does not make the population crowded; it is far below its earlier size.
If cod recovered like an r-selected species they would rebound fast; their slow recovery comes from late maturity and the changed food web.

why.correct: Upwelling supplies the nitrogen and phosphorus that limit phytoplankton. Without it, production at the base falls, and the effect passes up the food web: bottom-up control by a natural disturbance.
options: Warm water here means fewer nutrients, so phytoplankton decline rather than bloom.
Correct: less nutrient supply means less food at every level.
Sea lions are endotherms; the main effect on them is through their food supply.
The change is at the surface, where the phytoplankton live, so the food web is affected.

why.correct: Burning fossil fuels and burning or clearing forests both release carbon stored in organic matter as CO₂.
options: Adds CO₂: combustion of a fossil fuel.
Adds CO₂: burning and decay of the forest's carbon, and less photosynthesis afterward.
Removes CO₂: growing trees take in carbon by photosynthesis.
Wind turbines generate electricity without burning fuel.
Waterlogged peat decays slowly, so restoring a bog keeps carbon stored.

why.correct: This is thermal pollution. Gases dissolve less in warm water, and trout, as ectotherms, have a higher metabolic rate when the water is warmer, so oxygen supply falls just as demand rises.
options: Warm water holds less oxygen, not more.
Correct: less oxygen supply, more oxygen demand.
Temperature does not make water flow faster in this way.
Many algae grow faster in warmer water; the trout's problem is oxygen.

why.correct: Nutrients must arrive before the algae can bloom; the bloom must die before decomposers can use up the oxygen; low oxygen then drives off or kills animals.
When the input of a nutrient falls and algal growth falls with it, that nutrient was limiting. Less algae meant less decay and more oxygen in deep water.
options: In eutrophication, blooms come first and low oxygen follows when the algae decay.
Phosphate in detergents fed algae; it did not kill them, and blooms shrank when it was removed.
Correct: reducing the limiting nutrient reversed eutrophication.
Smaller blooms after cutting phosphorus show phosphorus was limiting; leftover blooms do not show nitrogen was.

why.correct: To build up from one level to the next, a chemical must stay in the body (fat-soluble) and last (persistent). Mercury, DDT and PCBs fit; quickly excreted or broken-down chemicals do not.
